question:
A 34-year-old male patient reports experiencing seizures that have been diagnosed as both "petit mal"
and "grand mal." His seizure episodes begin with sensations of déjà vu, epigastric "butterflies," and a
feeling of "unreality." These initial symptoms are followed by stiffening, leftward head turning, falling,
convulsions, and tongue biting. After each episode, he experiences difficult breathing and confusion
lasting over an hour. The patient's current treatment consists of phenobarbital, which he has taken for
10 years. Despite maintaining therapeutic drug levels, he continues to experience several seizures
annually. The medication causes side effects of drowsiness and lethargy. What is the most appropriate
therapeutic approach for this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Add a drug that is indicated for idiopathic
generalized seizures (B) Refer for temporal lobectomy (C) Initiate vagal nerve stimulation therapy (D)
Consider surgical evaluation for temporal lobe resection (E) Switch to a broad-spectrum antiepileptic
medication (F) Start cognitive behavioral therapy alongside medication (G) Substitute a drug that is
indicated for partial seizures (H) Add a second drug that targets GABA receptors (I) Add a
benzodiazepine for breakthrough seizures (J) Increase the dose of phenobarbital until seizures are
controlled
 A. Increase the dose of phenobarbital until seizures are controlled
B. Add a benzodiazepine for breakthrough seizures
C. Consider surgical evaluation for temporal lobe resection
D. Add a second drug that targets GABA receptors
E. Start cognitive behavioral therapy alongside medication
F. Switch to a broad-spectrum antiepileptic medication
G. Initiate vagal nerve stimulation therapy
H. Refer for temporal lobectomy
I. Substitute a drug that is indicated for partial seizures
J. Add a drug that is indicated for idiopathic generalized seizures
